I got this:

It's called a slipped disk. One of the disks in your spine, slips slightly out of alignment, pushing against the nerves of your spinal column - and it hurts like the fucking devil. This will be followed by swelling at the site of the injury, as your body will push the disk back into alignment. That also hurts as the swelling also puts pressure on the spinal cord.

The whole process usually takes three to four days, from the moment of slipping, to the disk becoming realigned.

Once it is realigned, the swelling and pain will go down, however, it is super super easy to slip it again, giving the impression that it is a permanent injury, and it can go on like that for years. Constantly slipping, then repairing, then slipping again. Pain, followed by you're fine, followed by pain again. Pain lasts for days, so it is difficult to see the cycle.

If you are walking during this time, the injury doesn't get fixed. Basically you are re-injuring yourself before the repair is done, and the whole process has to begin again.

It is necessary to get the disk realigned correctly, and then strengthen the area through special exercises designed to keep it aligned.

While the disk is slipped, walking will only make it worse. The pressure you are putting on your spine is pushing the disk up against the nerves, aggravating the injury. Actually, the best you can do is stretching and bed rest. Swimming can help.

A chiropractor can be most useful in identifying the exact disk involved, which is 90% of developing the correct physio therapy to repair the injury. Once you know what is broken, it is fairly easy to fix.

Meanwhile, immediate temporary relief is available via the following exercise: Lay on your back flat on the floor. Press your back into the floor. Then slowly pull your knees up to your chest, while still pressing your back flat onto the floor. You can use your arms to support your legs, and to tighten the stretch even further. Conduct this stretch slowly and hold it for a long time.

Even better if you have a helper who can hold your feet up and pull them back toward your head. Do this very slowly, and don't force anything. You can also use a rope to tie your feet to simulate the helper.

The idea is to stretch out your spine straight along the floor, while keeping it as flat as possible. You are pulling the bottom of your hips down and away from your spine - decompressing the spine. You want to make your spine longer, with more space between the disks. It takes time for the spine to let go and stretch - like many minutes, because you are stretching cartilage, not just muscle, and you have to both relax, and yet press the spine flat into the floor. When you do finally start to stretch your spine, the slipped disk usually will pop back into place. You may or may not feel it happen. This immediately removes the direct pressure from the nerve and offers immediate pain relief. The swelling at the injury site may also stop progressing from that point, because the injury is now repaired (sort of.)

You may even stand up again after this and feel completely normal, fully cured. You are not, but it can feel that way.

Surprisingly enough, increasing your abdominal muscle strength goes a very long way to keeping those disks in place. There are also smaller muscle groups that most people never use, in your lower to mid back, that can be greatly strengthened with exercises designed to do just these specific muscles. Physiotherapy has this knowledge.

Pool therapy as part of a physiotherapy training regime, using the water to support your body weight instead of your spine, can be useful to allow you to train the torso muscles without re-slipping the disk. Basically you walk laps of a pool in neck deep water. It's good exercise that is also very easy on the spinal cord.

What chiropractors do is to realign the bones - providing immediate pain relief. That works well. Physio therapists can strengthen the muscles to prevent re-injury, providing a long term cure, and teach you the exercises you can do at home if you run into the problem again.

Once you do get everything lined back up, then walking is excellent exercise for general toning of these muscle groups. Walking is a cardio exercise, and cardio works the abdominals perfectly. Walking strengthens the entire torso.

So try the floor stretch. If that doesn't work, get to the chiropractor and get a scan to identify the disk involved. After that, a combination of chiropractor and physio therapist can get you a permanent fix. I had a similar issue, and once I got the correct therapy, it was all resolved very quickly.
